summary: This standards-track document updates RFC 5280 to align with the 2008 specification for Internationalized Domain Names and to add support for internationalized email addresses in X.509 certificates. It was later replaced by RFC 9549.

eli5.summary: Names in digital ID cards can have letters from many languages. This updates the rules to handle them. It was later replaced by RFC 9549.

questions: how does x.509 handle internationalized domain names
what did rfc 8399 change in rfc 5280
how are international characters encoded in certificates
what is an a-label in punycode
subtitle: Updates to X.509 certificates for internationalized domain names and email addresses.

tldr.problem: X.509 certificates need to support domain names and email addresses that use non-ASCII characters from many languages. The original RFC 5280 lacked clear rules for encoding and comparing these internationalized names.
tldr.mechanism: This update specifies that internationalized domain names are encoded using Punycode (as ACE A-labels with the xn-- prefix) before being stored in certificates, and introduces rules for matching and validating these encoded names.
tldr.outcome: Certificates can now reliably represent internationalized domain names and email addresses according to the IDNA2008 standard. This was later replaced by RFC 9549.

facts.label: Character expansion
facts.value: Up to 5 ASCII characters per international character

today: RFC 8399 is a Proposed Standard. It updates RFC 5280 and was later superseded by RFC 9549.

sections.title: Introduction and Scope
sections.content:
RFC 8399 updates RFC 5280, the Internet X.509 Public Key Infrastructure (PKI) specification, to support Internationalized Domain Names (IDNs) and internationalized email addresses in certificates and certificate revocation lists (CRLs).

The problem is that X.509 certificates store domain names and email addresses using the IA5String type, which only supports ASCII characters. To accommodate names in other languages, the certificate specification needs clear rules for how to encode, store, and compare these international names. This update aligns with the IDNA2008 standard for internationalized domain names.
sections.eli5: Certificates need to handle names with accented letters and characters from other languages. This explains the rules for storing and comparing those names.

sections.title: Punycode Encoding and ACE Labels
sections.content:
The core technique is Punycode encoding. When an internationalized domain name (IDN) contains non-ASCII characters (called U-labels in Unicode form), each U-label must be converted to an ASCII-compatible encoding (ACE) A-label. An A-label is the Punycode-encoded form of the U-label with the prefix xn-- prepended.

For example, an IDN domain with international characters in Unicode form is encoded as a sequence of ASCII characters starting with xn-- and then placed in the certificate. When comparing DNS names in certificates, implementations perform case-insensitive exact matching on the A-label form.
sections.eli5: Non-English domain names get converted to a special ASCII code starting with xn-- before being stored in the certificate. This way, the certificate only contains ASCII characters.

sections.title: Where IDNs Appear in Certificates
sections.content:
IDNs can appear in several certificate extensions. These include the subjectAltName extension, the issuerAltName extension, the name constraints extension, the authority information access extension, the CRL distribution points extension, and others. All of these use the GeneralName type, and IDNs are stored in the dNSName field as ACE A-labels.

Distinguished names in the certificate subject and issuer fields can also include internationalized domain components. Each component must have all U-labels converted to A-labels before being stored as an IA5String attribute value.
sections.eli5: International domain names can appear in many different places inside a certificate. In each place, they are stored in the same encoded ASCII form.

sections.title: Internationalized Email Addresses
sections.content:
Email addresses with internationalized characters are handled in two cases. When the email address has an internationalized domain part but an ASCII local part (the part before the @), it goes in the rfc822Name field as an IA5String, with the domain part converted to A-labels. When the local part contains non-ASCII characters, the email address is placed in the SmtpUTF8Mailbox within the otherName field of GeneralName, using UTF-8 encoding as specified in RFC 8398.

For matching, conforming implementations perform an exact match on the local part and a case-insensitive match on the domain part (after converting A-labels back to U-labels for display).
sections.eli5: Email addresses with non-English characters go into certificates in a special format. If the sender's part is just ASCII, it uses one method. If the sender's part also has non-ASCII, it uses another.

sections.title: Validation and Implementation Considerations
sections.content:
Conforming Certificate Authorities should validate that IDNs are valid according to the IDNA2008 specification by checking all code points according to IDNA2008. Failure to use valid A-labels and U-labels may result in domain names that cannot be correctly represented in the Domain Name System.

Implementations should convert IDNs to Unicode before display, converting A-labels back to U-labels. An important consideration is that IDN ACE labels begin with the four extra characters xn--, and a single international character can require as many as five ASCII characters to represent in Punycode, significantly increasing memory requirements.
sections.eli5: Certificate authorities need to check that the encoded names are valid. Programs should convert them back to Unicode for humans to read. The encoded form takes more space than the original.
